newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU bond market could hold the key to euro's future.
newsitem.headline: EMU bond market could hold the key to euro's future.

text.p: The single European currency's ability to rival the dollar will depend, at least in part, on how quickly capital markets issue and trade debt in the new unit, the European Monetary Institute (EMI) said on Friday.

In its long-awaited review of the tools a European central bank will use to ensure the new currency's credibility, the EMI said the euro's strength would be affected greatly by rapid development of a euro-denominated debt market.

If governments inside monetary union harmonised issuing of national debt in the euro, "then you can get, very quickly, effective development of a euro-denominated bond market which then becomes an alternative to investment in the dollar," EMI president Alexandre Lamfalussy told reporters.
Economists reckon that a single currency launched even with only a handful of EU countries would result in the second largest bond market in the world after the United States.

If all 15 EU nations took part eventually, the potential outstanding debt would be 60 percent of the U.S. bond market and half as large again as the Japanese market, a recent Deutsche Bank study showed.

Lamfalussy also noted the possiblity of the euro becoming an "invoicing currency", a step that would further improve its attractiveness in international trade and propel it towards a major global reserve currency.
Various European centres are trying to build a vast euro bond market. Competition between Frankfurt, London and Paris has become vigorous in an array of financial products and services.

In an effort to gain an edge, the Paris-based futures and options exchange MATIF SA said on Friday it would cut commissions on financial contracts maturing after January 1, 1999 -- the euro's expected launch date.
MATIF also recently unveiled a comprehensive plan designed to capture the lion's share of business in euro bonds.

Not to be outdone, London's International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) recently agreed a link with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, which will allow continuous trading in LIFFE's three month Euromark futures contract, seen by many as the most liquid short term instrument in Europe.
In Germany, representatives of finance and industry in December formed a task force to work for changes and reforms to improve Frankfurt's competitive position as a financial centre.

The attractiveness of a euro bond market will also hinge on how much governments redenominate their outstanding national debt in the single currency. Countries such as France and Belgium have already announced that they plan to redenominate existing debt, but Germany is still undecided.
Economists also say differences in the breadth and liquidity of various national bond markets might make the transition towards one large euro market difficult to achieve quickly.

"It's unlikely to us that you will see an immediate harmonisation of European markets," said one London-based analyst. "What you may see instead are different issuers trying to compete for different parts of the market."

More important, say some observers, is whether a European central bank is perceived to be a strong inflation fighter. Such evaluation along with the economic conditions in 1999 will be key in establishing whether the euro is strong or weak against the dollar.
